pos: n. (Gaspard de Coligny, 1519–1572, Admiral of France, leader of the Huguenots, and first victim of the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre)
etymology: Persian through Latin Gaspar, treasurer; Coligny, the family's lordship in Burgundy.
biblical_def: Gaspard de Coligny was one of the great nobles of France, made Admiral in 1552. Captured by the Spanish at the fall of Saint-Quentin in 1557, he spent his captivity reading Scripture and the works of the Reformers, and came out a convinced Protestant. He became, with Louis de Condé, the political and military leader of the French Reformed churches through the first Wars of Religion, and after Condé's death in 1569 their chief commander. He also sponsored the first Protestant attempts at colonization in the New World, in Brazil in 1555 and in Florida in 1562–65, where the colony of Fort Caroline was destroyed by the Spanish. After the Peace of Saint-Germain in 1570 he came to court and gained the confidence of the young King Charles IX. On 22 August 1572, days after the marriage of Henry of Navarre to the king's sister had brought the Huguenot nobility to Paris, he was wounded by an assassin's shot. Before dawn on 24 August, Saint Bartholomew's Day, soldiers under the Duke of Guise broke into his lodgings, killed him, and threw his body from the window; the massacre of thousands across Paris and the provinces followed. He died commending his soul to Christ. He belongs with those of whom Psa 44:22 says, “for thy sake are we killed all the day long” (Psa 44:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an admiral as the commander of a fleet, and a massacre as the murder of numbers of men with cruelty.
webster_full: AD'MIRAL, n. A marine officer of the first rank; the commander of a fleet or navy.
MAS'SACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty.
HU'GUENOT, n. A French Protestant, of the reformed or Calvinistic communion.
scriptures: Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
Rom 8:36
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
Act 7:59
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.
corruption_summary: The Huguenot admiral murdered at the opening of the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Coligny's life carries the hard question of the French Reformation: whether the churches did right to defend themselves by arms under noble leaders. The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate answered that princes of the blood and great officers of the crown might lawfully resist a tyranny that sought to destroy the true religion, and Coligny acted on it.

The principle to recover is that such defence must never become trust in the arm of flesh. The Wars of Religion bound the French churches to the fortunes of nobles and armies, and when the nobility was butchered in a night the churches were left exposed. “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man” (Psa 118:8). Coligny's own end was a martyr's, like Stephen's: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59).
roots_summary: Hebrew harag (H2026), to kill; tsoan (H6629), sheep; Greek sphage (G4967), slaughter.
roots_lines: Hebrew chasah (H2620) — to trust, take refuge; Psalm 118:8.
usage: “for thy sake are we killed all the day long” (Psa 44:22) — 24 August 1572.
“we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Rom 8:36) — the Huguenot martyrs.
“It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man” (Psa 118:8) — the lesson of the wars.

pos: n. (the Atlantic port that was the stronghold of French Protestantism, besieged in 1572–73 and reduced by Richelieu in 1627–28)
biblical_def: La Rochelle was a prosperous, self-governing seaport on the Bay of Biscay whose citizens embraced the Reformed faith in the 1550s and 1560s, so that it became the capital and refuge of the Huguenots. In 1571 the seventh national synod of the French Reformed churches met there, with Theodore Beza presiding, and confirmed the confession of 1559, which has since been called the Confession of La Rochelle. After the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572, thousands of refugees fled to the city, and a royal army under the Duke of Anjou besieged it through the winter and spring of 1572–73 without taking it. Under the Edict of Nantes it was one of the fortified places granted to the Huguenots. In 1627, when the city allied itself with England against the crown, Cardinal Richelieu laid siege to it, building a great mole across the harbour to block relief by sea. The siege lasted fourteen months; when the city surrendered in October 1628, starvation had reduced its population from some twenty-seven thousand to about five thousand. The Peace of Alais in 1629 stripped the Huguenots of their fortresses and political assemblies. The defenders sang the psalm: “God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved” (Psa 46:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a siege as the setting of an army around a fortified place to compel its surrender.
webster_full: SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
REF'UGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
MOLE, n. A mound or massive work formed of large stones laid in the sea, extended before a port.
scriptures: Psa 46:5
God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.
Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: The Huguenot city of refuge, whose fall in 1628 ended Protestant arms in France.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. La Rochelle was a city of refuge and a fortress, and both roles are honourable. Its synod gave the French churches their confession, and its walls sheltered the survivors of 1572. The psalm the Huguenots sang there describes a defence that is finally God's: “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people” (Psa 125:2).

The principle to recover is the limit of walls. The churches' reliance on fortified towns and alliances with foreign powers made them a political party in the eyes of the crown, and when Richelieu broke the walls the party was broken. “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The Huguenots who survived the next century did so without a single fortress.
roots_summary: Hebrew qereb (H7130), midst; mot (H4131), to be moved; migdal (H4026), tower.
roots_lines: Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the midst, inward part; Psalm 46:5.
Hebrew mot (H4131) — to totter, be moved; Psalm 46:5.
usage: “God is in the midst of her” (Psa 46:5) — the psalm of the siege.
“tell the towers thereof” (Psa 48:12) — the Huguenot fortress.
“we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7) — what remained after 1628.

pos: n. (the Protestant insurgents of the Cévennes who rose against Louis XIV in 1702–1704)
etymology: Occitan camisa, a shirt, from the white shirts they wore in night attacks.
biblical_def: The Camisards were Protestant peasants and artisans of the Cévennes mountains and lower Languedoc who rose in arms against the persecution that followed the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. For seventeen years their region had endured forced conversions, the quartering of dragoons, the destruction of churches, the execution of preachers, and the sending of men to the galleys. Into this suffering came a wave of prophetic ecstasy: men, women, and even children, called inspirés, fell into trances and spoke in the name of the Spirit, calling the people to repentance and then to resistance. In July 1702 a band of them killed the Abbé du Chaila, the priest who directed the persecution in the Cévennes, at Pont-de-Montvert. The revolt spread; under leaders such as Jean Cavalier, a baker's apprentice, and Roland Laporte, a few thousand insurgents held off royal armies many times their number through guerrilla warfare in the mountains, while the king's commanders burned hundreds of villages. In 1704 Cavalier negotiated with Marshal Villars and left France; Roland was killed, and the rising was crushed by 1705. Their suffering recalls the saints of Heb 11:38, who “wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an insurgent as one who rises against lawful authority, and enthusiasm as a belief of private revelation.
webster_full: INSUR'GENT, n. A person who rises in opposition to civil or political authority.
ENTHU'SIASM, n. A belief or conceit of private revelation; the vain confidence or opinion of a person that he has special divine communications from the Supreme Being.
DRA'GOON, n. A soldier or mounted infantry.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.
I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Persecuted mountain Protestants who rose in arms under ecstatic prophets.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the prophetic ecstasy that drove the Camisard rising as error. The inspirés claimed direct revelations that Scripture does not warrant, and their utterances commanded killings. The apostolic rule is that “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (1Co 14:32), and the Lord's word through Jeremiah describes their kind: “I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran” (Jer 23:21). Their prophetism outlived the revolt as the French Prophets of London, with sad results.

That judgement must sit beside the persecution that provoked them, which was among the cruellest in Christian Europe. The principle to recover is the one Antoine Court drew from their ruin: the persecuted church is preserved not by prophets with swords but by the Word preached, the sacraments administered, and discipline restored. Christ's word to Peter stands over them: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).

roots_lines: Greek planao (G4105) — to wander, go astray; Hebrews 11:38.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to subject, be subject; 1 Corinthians 14:32.

“the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (1Co 14:32) — the test the inspirés failed.
“I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran” (Jer 23:21) — ecstasy without a call.

pos: n. (the underground French Reformed church between the Revocation of 1685 and the Edict of Toleration of 1787)
etymology: French Église du Désert, after the wilderness of Israel's wanderings and of Rev 12.
biblical_def: The Church of the Desert is the name French Protestants gave to their church during the century in which it was outlawed. The Edict of Fontainebleau in October 1685 revoked the Edict of Nantes, banished every Reformed pastor who would not abjure, forbade the laity to leave the kingdom, and ordered the demolition of their churches. Some two hundred thousand fled abroad despite the ban; those who remained were counted as new converts to Rome. But many met secretly to worship in what they called the desert: ravines, forests, caves, quarries, and mountain hollows, at night or before dawn, with sentries posted. Men caught at these assemblies were sent to the galleys for life, women imprisoned, children taken to be raised as Catholics, and preachers hanged or broken on the wheel. After the Camisard war, Antoine Court reorganized the scattered flocks from 1715, restoring synods, consistories, and a regular ministry trained at Lausanne. The church of the Desert held its confession and its psalms through three generations of persecution until Louis XVI's Edict of Versailles in 1787 restored civil status to Protestants. Its people took comfort in the woman of Revelation who “fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6), and obeyed the command not to forsake “the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a desert as a wilderness, a solitary place, and to abjure as to renounce upon oath.
webster_full: DES'ERT, n. A wilderness; a solitary place; an uninhabited tract of land.
ABJURE', v.t. To renounce upon oath; to recant or retract with solemnity.
ASSEM'BLY, n. A company or collection of individuals in the same place, usually for the same purpose; a congregation.
scriptures: Rev 12:6
And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.
corruption_summary: A century of secret worship in ravines and forests, under pain of the galleys.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Church of the Desert answers every modern claim that faithful worship depends on buildings, programmes, or the toleration of the state. For a hundred years the French Reformed met without any of them, sustained by Christ's promise: “where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20).

The principle to recover is that assembly is not optional. The Desert Protestants risked the galleys rather than give up public worship, because the apostle's command, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25), was to them a command and not a suggestion. A church that will not gather when gathering is easy has much to learn from one that gathered when it cost everything.
roots_summary: Greek eremos (G2048), wilderness; episunagoge (G1997), assembling together; Hebrew cheder (H2315), chamber.
usage: “fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6) — the church's name for itself.
“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — worship at the risk of the galleys.
“hide thyself as it were for a little moment” (Isa 26:20) — a century of hiding.

pos: n. (Antoine Court, 1695–1760, restorer of the French Reformed church in the Desert and founder of the seminary at Lausanne)
biblical_def: Antoine Court was born in the Vivarais in 1695, ten years after the Revocation, and grew up in the clandestine assemblies of the persecuted Protestants. As a youth he began to preach, and he saw what the Camisard war and its prophets had done to the churches: congregations scattered, discipline gone, and worship governed by the trances of the inspirés rather than by the Word. In August 1715, the month Louis XIV died, he gathered a handful of preachers and laymen in a quarry near Monoblet for the first synod of the Desert. That synod and those that followed forbade women to preach, set aside the claims of the prophets, restored elders and consistories, required that the sacraments be administered only by ordained ministers, and returned the churches to the Confession of La Rochelle and the old Discipline. In 1718 Court was himself ordained. In 1726 he founded, with the help of Swiss and foreign Protestants, a seminary at Lausanne to train pastors for the Desert, and from 1729 he directed it from exile; for decades almost every Desert pastor passed through it. He also collected the records of the persecution for history. His work was Paul's: “set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restoration as the act of replacing in a former state, and a synod as an ecclesiastical council.
webster_full: RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; reestablishment.
SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council, either provincial or general.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: The pastor who rebuilt a persecuted church on the Word, the sacraments, and discipline, not on prophets.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Court's first synod is one of the great acts of Reformed recovery. In a church that had come to depend on ecstatic prophets, he restored the ordinary means of grace and the ordinary offices, on the apostle's ground that “God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33). The synod's prohibition of women's preaching was the plain application of 1Co 14:34, and it was part of what made the Desert church a church again.

The principle to recover is that persecution does not suspend church order; it makes order more necessary. Court's seminary in exile obeyed the charge “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and the Desert churches outlived the persecution because they had pastors.
roots_summary: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930), to set in order; akatastasia (G181), confusion; eirene (G1515), peace.
roots_lines: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930) — to set further in order; Titus 1:5.
Greek leipo (G3007) — to be wanting, lack; Titus 1:5.

“God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33) — against the inspirés.
“commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the seminary at Lausanne.

pos: n. (Paul Rabaut, 1718–1794, pastor of the Desert at Nîmes for half a century)
etymology: Latin Paulus, small; French Rabaut, a family name.
biblical_def: Paul Rabaut was the son of a draper of Bédarieux who became a preacher of the Desert as a young man, studied under Antoine Court at Lausanne, and from 1741 was pastor of the outlawed Reformed church of Nîmes and its region for more than fifty years. For much of that time there was a price on his head. He lived in hiding, moved from house to house and from cave to cave, and preached to assemblies of thousands gathered at night in the countryside around Nîmes, baptizing, marrying, administering the Lord's Supper, and catechizing the young. He was the most respected leader of French Protestantism in the generation after Court, and he combined steadfast refusal to abandon the assemblies with unswerving loyalty to the crown and repeated petitions for toleration. His son, Rabaut Saint-Étienne, was a leader in the movement that won the Edict of Toleration in 1787 and sat in the National Assembly, where he pressed for religious liberty; he was guillotined in the Terror in 1793. The aged Paul Rabaut himself was imprisoned by the revolutionary authorities and released only after the fall of Robespierre, dying a few weeks later. He was the shepherd of Joh 10:11: “the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister having the charge of a church, and toleration as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship.
webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church.
PROSCRIP'TION, n. The act of dooming to death; outlawry.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
corruption_summary: A hunted pastor who preached to night assemblies for fifty years while praying for the king.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Rabaut's ministry combined two things moderns tend to separate: civil loyalty and ecclesiastical defiance. He honoured the king who outlawed him, as Peter commands, “Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17), and he would not stop preaching. The Desert pastors refused rebellion and refused silence, which is the apostolic posture under persecution.

The principle to recover is that the pastor's presence with his flock is itself a testimony. A minister with a price on his head who will not leave his people is the image of the Shepherd who lays down His life, and the fulfilment of the promise, “I will give you pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15).

roots_lines: Hebrew quwm (H6965) — to raise up, set up; Ezekiel 34:23.
usage: “the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11) — fifty years in hiding.
“pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15) — the Desert ministry.
“Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17) — loyalty without silence.

pos: n. (Marie Durand, 1711–1776, Huguenot prisoner held thirty-eight years in the Tower of Constance at Aigues-Mortes)
biblical_def: Marie Durand was born in the Vivarais, the daughter of a Protestant family whose home had been a meeting place for the Desert assemblies. Her brother Pierre Durand became a pastor of the Desert and a colleague of Antoine Court. Unable to take him, the authorities arrested his family; in 1730, aged about nineteen and newly married, Marie was imprisoned in the Tower of Constance, the great round tower of the walls of Aigues-Mortes in the Camargue, where Protestant women were held. Pierre was captured and hanged at Montpellier in 1732. Marie remained in the tower for thirty-eight years. She was offered release at any time if she would abjure her faith, and she refused. She became the leader and comforter of the women imprisoned with her, wrote letters on their behalf seeking help from Protestants abroad, and kept up their worship in the damp upper chamber. She was released in 1768, her health broken, and died eight years later. On the stone of the tower's rim is carved the word RESISTER, resist, which tradition attributes to her and her fellow prisoners. She is among the faithful of Rev 2:10: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines constancy as fixedness or firmness of mind, and imprisonment as confinement in a prison.
webster_full: CON'STANCY, n. Fixedness or firmness of mind; persevering resolution; especially applied to firmness of mind under sufferings.
IMPRIS'ONMENT, n. The act of putting and confining in prison; the state of being confined.
RESIST', v.t. To withstand; to strive against; to act in opposition.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
For the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners.
corruption_summary: A woman who refused a one-word abjuration for thirty-eight years in a prison tower.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Marie Durand is sometimes made into a symbol of resistance in the abstract, of conscience against power without regard to what the conscience held. She did not resist for liberty in general; she refused to deny Christ and His gospel by abjuring the Reformed faith for the religion of Rome. Her steadfastness was faith, like that of Paul and Silas in the Philippian jail, who “prayed, and sang praises unto God” (Act 16:25), and she kept such worship for decades.

The principle to recover is the church's duty to remember its prisoners, “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3). The Protestants of Switzerland, Holland, and England who sent help to the women of the tower obeyed that command, and the church today has prisoners of its own.
roots_lines: Greek stephanos (G4735) — a crown, victor's wreath; Revelation 2:10.
Greek desmios (G1198) — one bound, a prisoner; Hebrews 13:3.
usage: “be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — thirty-eight years in the tower.
“Remember them that are in bonds” (Heb 13:3) — the church's duty to its prisoners.
“the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners” (Psa 69:33) — the comfort of Aigues-Mortes.

pos: n. (the national synod of the French Reformed churches at Alençon in 1637, which examined and acquitted Moise Amyraut)
etymology: Greek sunodos, a meeting; Alençon, a town in Normandy.
biblical_def: The Synod of Alençon was the twenty-sixth national synod of the Reformed churches of France, meeting in 1637. Its most consequential business was the case of Moise Amyraut and Paul Testard, professors at the Academy of Saumur, whose writings, especially Amyraut's Brief Treatise on Predestination of 1634, had been charged with error. Amyraut taught a hypothetical universalism: that God decreed first to save all men through Christ on condition of faith, and then, since no man would believe of himself, decreed to give faith to the elect; so that Christ died for all sufficiently and conditionally, and for the elect effectually. Pierre du Moulin and others accused him of overturning the Canons of Dort. At Alençon, Amyraut and Testard explained themselves, affirming that faith is the gift of God to the elect alone and that the condition of the universal decree is one no man can fulfil without grace. The synod accepted their explanations and acquitted them, while forbidding them to use certain expressions and enjoining silence on the controversy. The silence was not kept, the debate continued for decades, and the Helvetic Consensus of 1675 was framed in part against Saumur. The Canons of Dort had said plainly what Christ said: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and acquittal as a judicial discharge from an accusation.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council, either provincial or general.
ACQUIT'TAL, n. A judicial setting free or deliverance from the charge of an offense.
HYPOTHET'ICAL, a. Including a supposition; conditional; assumed without proof.
scriptures: As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Joh 17:9
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: A French synod that acquitted Amyraut's hypothetical universalism with a warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Amyraut's scheme of a universal conditional decree as a departure from the Reformed doctrine of particular redemption, however orthodox his explanations at Alençon. A decree to save all on a condition God has decreed not to supply to all does not describe the Christ who prays “not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9), or the church He “hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

The synod's decision is a lesson in what acquittal with a warning accomplishes. It kept the peace for a season and left the question open for the next generation, which spent its strength on it while the crown prepared the Revocation. The principle to recover is that synods should decide doctrinal questions plainly, as Dort did, rather than enjoin a silence no one keeps.
roots_summary: Greek tithemi (G5087), to lay down; eklegomai (G1586), to choose; peripoieo (G4046), to purchase.
usage: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15) — the doctrine at issue.
“I pray not for the world” (Joh 17:9) — a particular intercession.
“purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — a definite redemption.

pos: n. (the national synods of the French Reformed churches held at Charenton near Paris, notably in 1631 and 1644–45)
etymology: Greek sunodos, a meeting; Charenton, the village east of Paris where the Reformed of the capital had their temple.
biblical_def: The Synod of Charenton names several national synods of the French Reformed churches held at Charenton, the village outside Paris where the Protestants of the capital were permitted to worship under the Edict of Nantes. Two of them made decisions of lasting importance. The synod of 1631 resolved that members of the Lutheran churches, since they agreed with the Reformed in the fundamentals of faith, might be admitted to the Lord's Table in French Reformed churches and might present children for baptism and stand as sponsors, without being required to abjure their own confession; it was one of the most notable acts of Protestant fellowship of the century. The synod of 1644–45 dealt with the teaching of Josué de la Place of Saumur, who had denied that the guilt of Adam's first sin is imputed immediately to his posterity, holding that men are counted guilty only because of the corruption of nature they inherit. The synod condemned the denial of the imputation of Adam's first sin, and the Helvetic Consensus later condemned La Place's position by name. The synods turned on Rom 5:18: “by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation” (Rom 5:18), and on the unity of the body: “we being many are one bread, and one body” (1Co 10:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imputation as the charging of the sins of Adam to his posterity.
webster_full: IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution. In theology, the charging of the sins of Adam to his posterity.
SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; union in religious worship, or in doctrine and discipline.
scriptures: Rom 5:18
Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: French synods that opened the Table to Lutherans and defended the imputation of Adam's sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names La Place's doctrine of mediate imputation as a corruption of the federal headship of Adam. Paul's parallel requires that as the righteousness of Christ is reckoned to His people immediately, so the guilt of Adam's first sin is reckoned to his: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1Co 15:22). Deny the one imputation and the other is put in question; Charenton saw that.

The synod of 1631 is a different lesson, in charity rather than precision. To receive Lutherans at the Table as brethren in the fundamentals, without demanding that they become Reformed, honoured the apostle's command to keep “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). The principle to recover is that a confessional church can be exact about doctrine and generous in fellowship at once.
usage: “by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation” (Rom 5:18) — the imputation La Place denied.
“as in Adam all die” (1Co 15:22) — the two heads.
“we being many are one bread” (1Co 10:17) — the Lutherans at the Table, 1631.

pos: n. (Claude Pajon, 1626–1685, French Reformed minister at Orléans whose doctrine of conversion by moral persuasion was condemned)
etymology: Latin Claudius, lame; French Pajon, a family name.
biblical_def: Claude Pajon studied at the Academy of Saumur under Amyraut, taught there briefly, and spent most of his ministry as pastor of the Reformed church at Orléans. He developed a doctrine of conversion that came to bear his name. Pajon held that the fall had darkened the mind but not destroyed the faculties, and that the Holy Spirit converts a sinner not by any immediate operation on the will or the heart, but by the Word presented to the mind in such circumstances that the understanding is persuaded, and the will necessarily follows the understanding. Grace is thus a work of providence arranging the means, and the Spirit works only through them, never directly. Pajon insisted that this was the doctrine of efficacious grace and that it gave all glory to God, since God arranges the circumstances that infallibly persuade. His opponents, led by Pierre Jurieu, answered that it reduced regeneration to moral suasion, left the will untouched by grace, and differed from Pelagianism only in its account of providence. Provincial synods condemned the teaching in the 1660s and 1670s. Against it stands the promise of a new heart: “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Eze 36:26), and the Lydia “whose heart the Lord opened” (Act 16:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persuasion as the act of influencing the mind by arguments, and regeneration as new birth by the grace of God.
webster_full: PERSUA'SION, n. The act of persuading; the act of influencing the mind by arguments or reasons offered.
REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued.
EFFICA'CIOUS, a. Effectual; productive of effects; producing the effect intended.
scriptures: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
corruption_summary: Conversion by moral persuasion: a Saumur theology that left the will untouched by grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Pajonism as a corruption of the doctrine of effectual calling. Scripture describes regeneration as a direct work of the Spirit on the heart, not merely as persuasion of the mind: the Lord opened Lydia's heart that she attended to what Paul spoke (Act 16:14), and Paul says “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13). A will that follows the intellect without being renewed is a will grace has not reached.

The modern form of the error is common wherever conversion is treated as the result of a sufficiently persuasive presentation. The principle to recover is the one the Canons of Dort confess: the Word is the instrument, but the Spirit Himself enters the inmost man, opens the closed heart, and makes the dead will alive, for “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44).
roots_summary: Hebrew leb (H3820), heart; eben (H68), stone; Greek dianoigo (G1272), to open.
roots_lines: Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, inner man; Ezekiel 36:26.
usage: “I will give you an heart of flesh” (Eze 36:26) — regeneration as a new heart.
“whose heart the Lord opened” (Act 16:14) — the Spirit's direct work.
“both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13) — grace reaching the will.
